opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the problem is that when we use words like "reading" or "understanding," we bring along all the connotations those words have for humans. When I say I've read a book, I mean I've built some kind of mental model of what it's about. I can tell you why the characters did what they did, I can relate it to my own experience, I can make inferences about things that weren't explicitly stated, and I can apply what I learned in a completely different situation.

When IBM said Watson "read" all of Wikipedia, or later that it was reading medical literature, what was actually happening was very different. The system was processing text statistically. It was finding correlations between words and phrases and matching patterns that turned out to be useful for answering certain kinds of questions, like Jeopardy clues. That's an impressive engineering achievement, and I don't want to diminish it. But it's not reading in any sense that a person would recognize if they looked under the hood.

The danger is that this language sets up expectations the system can't meet. People hear that Watson understands medical literature, and they assume it can reason about a patient the way a knowledgeable doctor would. Then it goes into hospitals and it doesn't work nearly as well as advertised, because it was never understanding in that sense. It was brittle. It didn't have the common sense or the background knowledge that gives human understanding its flexibility.

Drew McDermott wrote about this back in the 1970s. He called these "wishful mnemonics." We name a program component "understand" or "learn" or "goal," and then we, and the public, start believing the program actually does those things. I think AI as a field has always been prone to this, and it has real consequences. It distorts public perception, it affects funding and hype cycles, and it can even mislead researchers themselves about how much progress has really been made. So I try to be careful, and to encourage others to be careful, about the words we use.

r001.rationale: The response says calling Watson a reader imports human connotations and can lead people to assume it understands text as a person would, though it is statistically processing patterns.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the problem is that words like "reading" and "understanding" carry a huge amount of baggage from how we use them for humans. When I say I've read a book, I mean I've built up some kind of mental model of what's in it. I can relate it to things I already know, I can draw inferences that go well beyond what's literally on the page, I can tell you what the author probably intended, and I can apply what I learned to situations the book never mentioned. That's what understanding means for us.

When IBM said Watson "reads" millions of documents, what it was actually doing was something much more like sophisticated pattern matching over text. It could find statistical associations, it could pull out answers to Jeopardy-style questions because it had learned which strings of words tend to co-occur with which other strings. That's genuinely impressive engineering, but it's not reading in the sense that any of us mean when we use the word. And the trouble is that the word does a lot of work in people's minds. If you hear that a system has read all of the medical literature, you naturally assume it has the kind of grasp of medicine that a person who had read all of that would have. And then you're surprised, as a lot of hospitals were, when it turns out the system has no idea what a tumor actually is, or what it means for a treatment to be dangerous.

I think of this as part of what I've called the fallacy of wishful mnemonics. Drew McDermott coined the term back in the seventies. We name our programs and their components with words like "understand," "learn," "goal," and then we start to believe the program really has those properties, just because we gave it that label. The label becomes a kind of self-deception. And it's not only a marketing problem, though it certainly is that. It also affects how researchers think about their own systems, and it affects how the public and policymakers calibrate their trust.

So I'd say the misleading part is that these words invite you to assume the system has all the other capabilities that come bundled with understanding in humans, like common sense, like robustness to slight changes in phrasing, like knowing when it doesn't know something. And those are precisely the capabilities these systems tend to lack. The gap between what the word promises and what the system can actually do is where a lot of the overpromising and disappointment in AI comes from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says calling Watson’s activity “reading” leads people to assume it has the human-like grasp of the text that a person would, though its actual operation is pattern matching.

astra-6.text:
What I find misleading is that words like “reading” and “understanding” carry a lot of assumptions from our experience with people. If I tell you that someone has read a medical textbook and understood it, you assume they can explain what they learned, connect it to other knowledge, and recognize when it applies to a new situation.

A system like Watson can process text and use patterns in it to produce answers, sometimes very successfully. But that success doesn’t by itself establish that it understands the text in that broader sense. The danger is that we see an impressive performance on a particular task and attribute a whole collection of human abilities to the system that haven’t actually been demonstrated.

So I think we need to describe more precisely what these systems can do, and where they fail, rather than letting a word like “understanding” do all the explanatory work.

r001.rationale: The candidate says “reading” carries human assumptions and explains that Watson’s text processing does not establish broader human-like understanding, identifying the unwarranted inference.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, words like “reading” and “understanding” carry a lot of baggage. When we say a person has read something, we assume they’ve connected it to what they know about the world, can draw inferences from it, and can recognize when it doesn’t make sense. If we say Watson reads millions of documents, people naturally attribute those same abilities to it.

Watson was very good at finding patterns in language and using them to answer Jeopardy! questions. That’s an impressive accomplishment. But it doesn’t establish that it understands those questions in the way a person does. The misleading part is taking a system’s success on a particular task and using language that suggests a much broader, more flexible understanding than we’ve actually demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response says calling Watson a reader leads people to attribute human abilities to it, and clarifies that its task success does not establish understanding in the human sense.
